pr_title: ENH: Implemented optional initializer for pd.concat (#40820)
pr_body:
- [x] closes #40820 
- [x] tests added / passed (passed on azure checks)
- [x] Ensure all linting tests pass, see [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/dev/development/contributing.html#code-standards) for how to run them
- [x] whatsnew entry

A proposed solution for issue #40820, to accept an optional argument ``initializer`` which allows for concatenating empty sequences and return the object passed to initializer -- which can be useful for cases where users are running pd.concat on sequence variables which might potentially be empty -- and would like the result of the concatenation to be initialized to an empty Series/DataFrame

The new argument is made optional, and the ValueError is still thrown for cases where the ``initializer`` is not specified -- this should maintain expected behaviour / backward compatibility
pr_comments: As stated in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/40820#issuecomment-834604151, I don't think `concat` should be responsible for determining the return type for an empty input.

> @yushao2 sympathize with the issue. we don't anything like this and don't think have this magically just work is a good idea. not to mention adding complexity.

no worries, I will rescind the PR :) cheers

issue_context.title: ENH: Make concat succeed on empty list.
issue_context.body:
#### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Yes, `pd.concat([])` currently raises the exception, ValueError("No objects to concatenate").

#### Describe the solution you'd like

To be correct on all input sizes, it should return an empty DataFrame.

#### API breaking implications

Obviously, concat will no longer detect empty data.  However, empty data will detect itself.

#### Additional context

The concatenation operation is for lists what addition is for numbers.  Concatenation of an empty list should produce an empty dataframe, because the empty dataframe represents `0`.  Consider
```
sum([])
```
which python evaluates to 0.

This makes concatenation and sum commute, `sum([1] + []) == sum([1]) + sum([])`.

This already works for an empty dataframe:
```
pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({'A':[1]}), pd.DataFrame()])
```
if is very odd for concat([]) not to produce a DataFrame, since its input has the correct type.
comments:
I guess it is not clear what should be the return type.
If we concat dataframes, then the function returns a dataframe.
Similarly, for series objects it returns a series.
However, what should we return in case of an empty input?

> I guess it is not clear what should be the return type.
> If we concat dataframes, then the function returns a dataframe.
> Similarly, for series objects it returns a series.
> However, what should we return in case of an empty input?

I agree, and if Series is to be interpreted as a 'simpler' object (i.e. df["colA"] returns a Series not a DataFrame), then arguably one might suggest returning a Series rather than a DataFrame, if anything at all is returned.

Sounds like a solution would be for concat([]) to return a new object type representing both empty Series and empty DataFrames.  Perhaps there's a base class that makes sense there - I don't know enough to say.

For now, I just create my own `concatDF` function that only works on DataFrames.

> Sounds like a solution would be for concat([]) to return a new object type representing both empty Series and empty DataFrames. Perhaps there's a base class that makes sense there - I don't know enough to say.
> 
> For now, I just create my own `concatDF` function that only works on DataFrames.

Here's an idea, incorporating an optional initializer for the pd.concat function, similar to reduce:

https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.reduce

Otherwise, it seems like the base class is generic.NDFrame:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/3cce96f515917170ea9bce731ffcc913750464b8/pandas/core/generic.py#L187

> Sounds like a solution would be for concat([]) to return a new object type representing both empty Series and empty DataFrames. Perhaps there's a base class that makes sense there - I don't know enough to say.
> 
> For now, I just create my own `concatDF` function that only works on DataFrames.

I created a PR for this for the first solution mentioned -- feel free to take a look and share your thoughts.

It's my first time contributing to this project so I'm sorry if I've made any mistakes.

Thanks!

I find the current behavior correct as is.

For reference `np.concatenate` also raises a similar error as `pd.concat`

```
In [1]: np.concatenate([])
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-1-7806ca832c55> in <module>
----> 1 np.concatenate([])

<__array_function__ internals> in concatenate(*args, **kwargs)

ValueError: need at least one array to concatenate
```

And I believe it's more explicit for the user to decide what to do in code flow if they get to a `pd.concat([])` situation.

So I'd be -1 on any changes here.

Thanks for the suggestion, but also from the review on a proposal PR https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/41355#pullrequestreview-654681587, I think this behavior is best left for the user to decide manually what the result of empty concatenation should be. Closing.

review_comments: I suggest that this is moved to a separate test.

In my opinion the new parameters are better be introduced using keyword-only argument notation (for better maintainability in future).

```
def func(first, second, *, keyword_only=None):
```

I understand that there are already multiple kwargs, which are not keyword-only and can technically be passed as positional, but maybe it is a good moment to start (question to core developers)?

@ivanovmg, could you provide an example of how the function signature would look like with keyword-only argument notation?

Admittedly I'm still relatively new to writing production code so it would really help if you could show me an example of how it would be done. Thanks!

Like this:
```
def concat(
    objs: Iterable[NDFrame] | Mapping[Hashable, NDFrame],
    axis=0,
    join="outer",
    ignore_index: bool = False,
    keys=None,
    levels=None,
    names=None,
    verify_integrity: bool = False,
    sort: bool = False,
    copy: bool = True,
    *,  # <- note star here
    initializer: NDFrame | None = None,
) -> FrameOrSeriesUnion:
```

But, again, I have not seen this approach widely used among the code base, so I am not sure what are the core development team preferences.
nevertheless, learnt something new today. Thank you :)
It seems that there is an extra newline between ``copy`` and ``initializer`` docstrings.
